rashi:a6.1: According to Rabbi Zeira, it is impossible to identify its prohibition: since both of them have been eaten.
rashi:a6.2: According to Rav Naḥman, the prohibition was established: from the outset, and he is liable.
rashi:a11.1: Rabbi Meir deems him obligated: on account of slaughtering outside [the Temple], even though one could say: perhaps he did not eat forbidden fat, and this guilt offering is non-sacred; for he does not require the prohibition to be established.
rashi:a11.2: And the Rabbis deem him exempt: since the prohibition was not established, for perhaps it is non-sacred.
rashi:a12.1: But why: was he distressed that he had not said to him “It is Rabbi Meir”? He should have said to him, as in his earlier answers, “It is Rabbi Eliezer.”
rashi:a12.2: He holds in accordance with the approach of Rabbi Eliezer: that is why [Rabbi Meir] deems him obligated, since he does not require an established prohibition. And that he had not said to him “It is Rabbi Eliezer” did not trouble him, since [Rava] could have known that by himself.
rashi:a13.1: [Rashi’s heading reads “Rava said”; the daf reads Rabba bar Avuh.] Even though we said above that he is exempt, because we require two pieces, that was not said as everyone’s opinion; for Rabbi Eliezer deems him obligated, since he says that a person may volunteer, etc., and one cannot say here that he is bringing non-sacred animals into the [Temple] courtyard. Here he is certainly obligated, since he came into a situation of uncertainty.
rashi:a14.1: A person may volunteer, etc.: Rabbi Eliezer’s reason is explained in the Gemara in the last chapter (below, Keritot 25a).
rashi:a15.1: Rav Ashi said: what we require, some measure of prohibition even according to Rabbi Eliezer, is said according to Bava ben Buta, who [is reported] in the last chapter (ibid.) to have brought a provisional guilt offering every day except the day after Yom Kippur. He said: By this Abode [the Temple]! If they would let me, I would bring one; but they say to me: Wait until you enter into a situation of uncertainty. That is, wait until tomorrow, when there is some uncertainty that perhaps [one incurred] a sin offering today. But on the day after Yom Kippur there is no concern for this, since Yom Kippur has atoned for his uncertainty, as we say in the last chapter (ibid.): those liable to provisional guilt offerings over whom Yom Kippur has passed are exempt. And according to [Bava ben Buta] we require some uncertainty, such as a single piece, even according to Rabbi Eliezer. But the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer in the last chapter (ibid.) and say that one brings a provisional guilt offering only for something whose intentional violation is punishable by karet, so that if he brings one he would be bringing non-sacred animals into the courtyard, exempt him here too, for we specifically require [two pieces], as we read “mitzvot.”
rashi:a16.1: And the same if a dog: ate the second, or a raven, the Jew is liable, since at the time he ate it was one piece of two pieces.
rashi:a16.2: Exempt: since there are not two pieces.
rashi:a16.3: And Rabbi deems him obligated: since he does not require two pieces.
rashi:a17.1: And the second intentionally: that he knew it was uncertain.
rashi:a17.2: Liable: to a provisional guilt offering for the first, since it was unwitting and was one of two pieces.
rashi:a17.3: Exempt: since at the time of the unwitting eating there were not two pieces.
tosafot:a11.1: One who slaughters a provisional guilt offering outside, Rabbi Meir deems him obligated: And even though Rabbi Meir says below, in chapter HaMevi (Keritot 23b), that if his uncertainty became known to him [i.e., it was resolved], the animal goes out and grazes in the flock, meaning that it goes out to non-sacred status, here it speaks of before it became known to him, when the name “guilt offering” is still upon it.
tosafot:a11.2: And the Rabbis deem him exempt: these are not the Rabbis below, in chapter HaMevi (ibid.), who disagree with Rabbi Meir and say that it grazes until it becomes blemished, is sold, and its money goes to [the fund for] voluntary offerings; for if so, it is fully consecrated and one is liable for slaughtering it outside. Rather, these Rabbis hold like Rabbi Meir and go further than Rabbi Meir, exempting him even before it became known to him.
tosafot:a13.1: In brief: “We have arrived at the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis… why specifically when he ate it?” Tosafot ask: What is the objection? Indeed he could volunteer, but here [Rav] makes the guilt offering an obligation for his sin, and teaches that he must bring it and that we do not require one piece of two. And further: why did the Gemara not raise this objection earlier, against Rabbi Eliezer’s ruling on the koy? They answer that this is the objection: perforce the Rabbi Eliezer here is not the Rabbi Eliezer of the koy, for then what would Rav Naḥman be teaching us? Rather, above [in the koy baraita] the reading is Rabbi Elazar, and here it is Rabbi Eliezer, the disputant of Rabbi Yehoshua, as the passage shows. So the Gemara asks: from where do you know that Rabbi Eliezer obligates a provisional guilt offering for one piece? We find that Rabbi Eliezer does not require two pieces only because he says one may volunteer a provisional guilt offering every day; if so it is not an obligation, and then even if he did not eat. The answer, “Rabbi Eliezer according to Bava ben Buta,” refers to the day after Yom Kippur, as Rashi explained. Tosafot then ask whether Rav is teaching that Rabbi Eliezer holds the written form of the text is authoritative, “mitzvot” being written [defectively], since Rabbi Eliezer holds so in Kiddushin (18b) on “bevigdo vah”; if so, let it teach: if he ate it, an obligation; if not, a gift. They answer that perforce Rav did not cite him for that reason, for then he could have cited many others who hold so; and even if Rabbi Eliezer holds so elsewhere, here he holds the vocalized reading is authoritative, for the reason explained earlier. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: What is the reason of Rav? He holds: with two pieces, the prohibition was established, since one of them is certainly forbidden fat; therefore he is liable. With one piece, the prohibition was not established, since it may be permitted fat.
gershom:a2.1: What is the difference between “the prohibition was established” and “it is impossible to identify its prohibition”? And [between these and] Rava, who requires “mitzvot”?
gershom:a3.1: According to Rava, there is no “mitzvot” at the time the Jew ate the second, since the first is no longer there, for the gentile ate it.
gershom:a4.1: And likewise according to Rabbi Zeira he is exempt: since when the Jew ate the second, nothing remained there, and it is impossible to identify the prohibition, what he ate.
gershom:a5.1: And according to Rav Naḥman he is liable, since the prohibition was established: for there were two pieces at the outset, and one of them was forbidden.
gershom:a6.1: Rava raised an objection to Rav Naḥman: but the koy, the uncertain nine-month child, and the uncertain menstruant are each not a case of two pieces, and you cannot say the prohibition was established, and yet they are liable to a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:a7.1: One who slaughters a provisional guilt offering outside: a provisional guilt offering is of uncertain status, sacred or non-sacred; for if he ate forbidden fat it is a sacred guilt offering, and if he ate permitted fat it is non-sacred. Rabbi Meir obligates him to bring a provisional guilt offering, since he slaughtered outside something that is possibly sacred. Evidently Rabbi Meir does not require establishment, since he obligates even for one piece.
gershom:a8.1: And the Rabbis deem him exempt: since they require establishment.
gershom:a9.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom reads Rabbi Elazar here.] And why did he say to him “It is Rabbi Meir”? Let him say to him “It is Rabbi Elazar” too. Indeed he could have said that; but this teaches us that Rabbi Meir holds the approach of Rabbi Elazar, who does not require establishment of the prohibition.
gershom:a10.1: We have arrived at the dispute of Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis, who disagree in the mishna of our last chapter. According to Rabbi Elazar, who says a person may volunteer a provisional guilt offering every day, he brings a provisional guilt offering for this too. According to the Rabbis, who say one brings a provisional guilt offering only for something whose intentional violation is punishable by karet and whose unwitting violation requires a sin offering, here, since its intentional eating is not punishable by karet, as it may be permitted fat, one does not bring a provisional guilt offering for it. [The printed text adds an editor’s note: this reason for the Rabbis is puzzling, since it would apply equally to one piece of two; perhaps he means one must eat something that, if certain, carries karet; the matter requires study.] According to Rabbi Eliezer, why specifically when he ate it? Even if he did not eat it he may also bring one, as we learned: Rabbi Eliezer, etc.
gershom:a11.1: Rav Ashi said: what it teaches, “and he ate it,” is Rabbi Eliezer according to Bava ben Buta.
gershom:a12.1: As we learned: but he said to him: Wait: that you should not bring a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:a13.1: Until you enter into a situation of uncertainty: until you do something that carries an uncertain obligation of a sin offering, for example eating a piece that may be forbidden fat or may be permitted fat, or the like. And the one who said this to him is Rabbi Eliezer. Therefore he says “and he ate it,” which is a situation of uncertain liability to a sin offering. This teaching about Bava ben Buta is in the last chapter: They said about Bava ben Buta that he would volunteer a provisional guilt offering every day except for the one day after Yom Kippur, since Yom Kippur atones in place of a provisional guilt offering, and on the day after Yom Kippur he himself knows that whatever he sinned was yesterday, and today he has not yet sinned. He said: By this Abode! If they would let me, I would bring one even on the day after Yom Kippur; but he said to me: Wait, etc., as we said.
gershom:a14.1: A Jew came and ate the first: he is liable, since at the time he ate there were two pieces.
gershom:a15.1: And Rabbi deems him obligated: since he holds the prohibition was established.
gershom:a16.1: He ate the first unwittingly and the second intentionally, he is liable: to a provisional guilt offering for the first, since at the time of the unwitting eating there were two pieces.
gershom:a17.1: The first intentionally and the second unwittingly, he is exempt: since at the time of the unwitting eating there was only one piece.
gershom:a18.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “And Rabbi Meir deems him obligated”; the daf reads “Rabbi”.] In any case, since at the outset there were two pieces, the prohibition was established.
gershom:a19.1: And the second, not by law: is liable, for at the time of his eating there were not two pieces.
gershom:a20.1: But if you say the second is exempt, you have established the first as [certainly] liable to a sin offering: since the second is exempt, learn from it that he ate the piece of permitted fat and his fellow ate the piece of forbidden fat and is liable to a sin offering; and that is not so, for he does not know which one he ate. And whose is this latter clause?
gershom:a21.1: If it is Rabbi, it is by law, fully by law: that the second should be liable, since he holds the prohibition was established at the outset.
gershom:a22.1: And if it is the Rabbis: why is the second liable?
gershom:a23.1: Because the first should not be established as liable to a sin offering, shall we tell the second, who is exempt, to bring non-sacred animals into the courtyard? For his provisional guilt offering would be non-sacred, since he is exempt from an offering.
gershom:a24.1: Rav Ashi said: as for the second bringing a provisional guilt offering even though it is not by law…
rashi:b1.1: It is Rabbi Eliezer: therefore one cannot say they are non-sacred animals in the courtyard.
rashi:b1.2: And stipulate: if the first ate permitted fat, the second [certainly ate] forbidden fat; and if he ate forbidden fat, out of the uncertainty let it be an atonement for him, to protect him until it becomes known to him and he brings a sin offering; and if not, let it be a gift offering.
rashi:b2.1: And he was informed: that it is uncertain.
rashi:b2.2: Just as: if it became known to him at the end that they were all certainly forbidden fat, he would certainly bring a sin offering for each one, since the intervening knowledge of uncertainty divides them into separate sin offerings, as it is not a single lapse of awareness.
rashi:b2.3: So too he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one: as long as certain knowledge has not become known to him.
rashi:b4.1: Here Rabbi taught: as I explained [above].
rashi:b8.1: But if that is so, he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat before Yom Kippur and an olive-bulk of forbidden fat after Yom Kippur: and both in a single lapse of awareness.
rashi:b8.2: In place of a provisional guilt offering: as it is taught in the last chapter (below, Keritot 25a): those liable to provisional guilt offerings over whom Yom Kippur has passed are exempt. So it is like knowledge of uncertainty.
rashi:b9.1: Perhaps: what we say, that Yom Kippur atones, is where it became known to him that he ate possibly forbidden fat.
rashi:b9.2: We learned “informed or not informed”: in the first chapter of Shevuot (12b) the Gemara explains: whether his uncertainty became known to him before Yom Kippur or did not become known to him, Yom Kippur atones. Evidently it atones even though it did not become known to him at all.
rashi:b12.1: He ate and drank in one lapse of awareness: on Yom Kippur.
rashi:b12.2: He is liable to only one: since drinking is included in eating.
rashi:b12.3: That he could gain knowledge: that is, there is enough time that he could have been informed; and since there is a stretch of Yom Kippur in between long enough for knowledge, that stretch stands in place of uncertain knowledge, as with a provisional guilt offering.
rashi:b13.1: It is the Rabbis: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Eliezer [the baraita on this daf reads Rabbi Elazar].
rashi:b16.1: He ate today: of consecrated property worth half a peruta.
rashi:b16.2: Derived benefit: from something that is not edible.
rashi:b16.3: And from now until three years: and in a single lapse of awareness.
rashi:b17.1: But Yom Kippur atoned for him: the Yom Kippur in between, for the first half-measure. And if knowledge of uncertainty divides, Yom Kippur was like knowledge of uncertainty; so why do they combine?
rashi:b22.1: That is why he ties the guilt offering to the sin offering: just as certain knowledge in between would divide into separate sin offerings, as it is written: “Or if his sin be made known to him” (Leviticus 4:23), so knowledge of uncertainty divides into separate guilt offerings, and he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one. But according to Reish Lakish he should have tied the sin offering to the guilt offering: just as knowledge of uncertainty divides into guilt offerings, so it divides into sin offerings, and when it becomes known to him at the end he brings a sin offering for each one; for the main [source] of knowledge of uncertainty is written regarding the guilt offering.
rashi:b23.1: One impure and one pure: and it is not known which is impure and which is pure.
rashi:b23.2: And did not enter: the Temple.
rashi:b23.3: On the second and entered: the Temple.
rashi:b23.4: Liable: for entering the Temple, since either way there is certain knowledge that he is impure, for he walked on both.
rashi:b24.1: On the second and entered: and when he entered after the second, the impurity of the first entry was hidden from him; he is liable.
tosafot:b7.1: But isn’t it taught: whatever is divided, etc.: Even though Rabbi Yehuda says this above (Keritot 15b), nevertheless it does not imply that Rabbi disagrees with him on this. According to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, this is its explanation: whatever is divided into separate sin offerings, such as forbidden fat and blood, or piggul and notar, is divided into separate guilt offerings, so that he must bring a provisional guilt offering for each one; but it does not deal with knowledge. And according to Rava too, this is its explanation: whatever is divided into sin offerings by certain knowledge is divided into guilt offerings by knowledge of uncertainty.
tosafot:b8.1: But if that is so, he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat before Yom Kippur and an olive-bulk after Yom Kippur: For now there are two guilt offerings: for the eating of forbidden fat before Yom Kippur, Yom Kippur atoned in place of a guilt offering, and for the eating of forbidden fat after Yom Kippur he brings a guilt offering. So now that there are two guilt offerings, if he learned afterward about both, would he likewise bring two sin offerings? But he ate them in a single lapse of awareness! Rather, he does not bring [two]. If so, learn from it that this principle, “whatever is divided, etc.,” does not hold, for here there are two guilt offerings and only one sin offering.
tosafot:b9.1: He said to him: perhaps Yom Kippur atones only if he was informed: and now there are two sin offerings, like the two guilt offerings. Rava bar Rav Ḥanan said to him: Terada [so Tosafot’s text reads here; the daf has “Rava said to him”, and gives the word terada below to Rabba bar bar Ḥana]: Rava bar Rav Ḥanan was Abaye’s companion, as in chapter Keitzad Mevarekhin (Berakhot 46b).
tosafot:b10.1: It chose an olive-bulk of forbidden fat in the morning of Yom Kippur, and not something permitted, for which he would be liable to an offering on account of Yom Kippur itself, on which eating is forbidden, because then it would have needed to choose the measure of a large date, which is the measure for eating on Yom Kippur; it chose a small measure, and so it chose an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, which is less.
gershom:b1.1: [The printed text marks that the notes up to here belong to 18a.] It is Rabbi Eliezer, who says a person may volunteer a provisional guilt offering every day. Since he may bring one either way, we say to the second: Bring a provisional guilt offering and stipulate: if the first ate permitted fat, then he ate forbidden fat, and let this guilt offering be his atonement; and if not, let it be a gift offering.
gershom:b2.1: Rabbi says: I say, just as he brings a sin offering for each and every one: when he ate possibly forbidden fat and learned that he had eaten possibly forbidden fat, and again ate possibly forbidden fat and learned that it was possibly forbidden fat, and again ate possibly forbidden fat and learned that he had certainly eaten forbidden fat: since at the end there was certain knowledge, he brings a sin offering for each one. And just as he brings a sin offering for each one, so he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one.
gershom:b3.1: Here Rabbi taught: knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings. Even though the earlier pieces of knowledge were knowledge of uncertainty, since the last was certain knowledge, those earlier uncertain ones also divide into sin offerings. That is why he says: just as he brings a sin offering for each one, so he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one.
gershom:b4.1: And Rava says: knowledge of uncertainty does not divide into sin offerings at all. Rather, this is what it teaches: just as, if he had certain knowledge between each one, he would bring a sin offering for each one, so if he had knowledge of uncertainty, he therefore brings a provisional guilt offering for each one, but not sin offerings.
gershom:b5.1: And do you not hold that knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings? Rather, you hold that knowledge of uncertainty does not divide into sin offerings, and he brings one sin offering for the last, certain knowledge. If so, why does he bring a provisional guilt offering for each one? But isn’t it taught: the principle, etc.?
gershom:b6.1: But if that is so, he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat before Yom Kippur and another olive-bulk after Yom Kippur, in a single lapse of awareness.
gershom:b7.1: And Yom Kippur stands in place of a provisional guilt offering: as we learned in our last chapter: those liable to provisional guilt offerings, after Yom Kippur, are exempt. And since this Yom Kippur stands in place of a provisional guilt offering, it is like knowledge of uncertainty. Since you said knowledge of uncertainty divides, would he likewise bring two sin offerings? Why?
gershom:b8.1: But he ate them in a single lapse of awareness: and for a single lapse of awareness he is liable to only one sin offering.
gershom:b9.1: Abaye said to him: who shall tell us that Yom Kippur atones in place of a provisional guilt offering even though it did not become known to the owner that he ate? Perhaps it atones only where it became known to him that he ate an uncertainty, and here it did not become known to him.
gershom:b10.1: He said to him: Tarara: lazy one. [In Rabbeinu Gershom’s text Rava’s reply here opens with this word.]
gershom:b11.1: We learned “informed or not informed”: in our first chapter of Shevuot: for other transgressions punishable by death or karet, informed or not informed, positive or negative commandments, Yom Kippur atones, even though it did not become known to him.
gershom:b12.1: What if he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat in the morning on Yom Kippur and an olive-bulk of forbidden fat in the afternoon: would he likewise be liable to two sin offerings? For the part of Yom Kippur in between atones for him in place of a provisional guilt offering, and it should be like knowledge of uncertainty in between, and he should be liable to two sin offerings. And we hold that he is not, since they were in a single lapse of awareness.
gershom:b13.1: Abaye said to him: and from where do we know that Yom Kippur atones at every hour, even part of the day, that is, so that it would be [like] knowledge of uncertainty? Perhaps it does not atone until there is the entire day without sin.
gershom:b14.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom reads that Rava said this; the daf gives it to Rabba bar bar Ḥana.] Rava said to him: Tarara! One who encountered, etc.: so even part of the day atones, and by your words he should be liable to two sin offerings. And likewise, between eating and drinking it is impossible that there was not a little time, and that bit of Yom Kippur atoned for him, as it stands in place of a provisional guilt offering; and yet it teaches: he is liable only, etc.
gershom:b15.1: They say: when Rabbi Zeira said that knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings, it was according to Rabbi, as he said: here Rabbi taught. And what it teaches, that he is liable to only one sin offering, is the Rabbis, who do not hold that knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings.
gershom:b16.1: But from the latter clause it is Rabbi, as it teaches: if he drank fish brine or morayes, he is exempt, since it is made not for drinking but for dipping, and does not revive the spirit; but if he drank vinegar he is liable, since it revives the spirit. Evidently the first clause is also Rabbi.
gershom:b17.1: They say: no; the latter clause is Rabbi and the first clause is the Rabbis, and it is not difficult.
gershom:b18.1: He ate today: of consecrated property, and ate of consecrated property tomorrow; or derived benefit from consecrated property today and derived benefit tomorrow; or ate today and derived benefit tomorrow, or the reverse; and even from now until three years, that he did not complete [the value of] a peruta for three years.
gershom:b19.1: From where that they combine with each other: to a peruta, and to [liability for] misuse? The verse states “commits a misuse”: it extended.
gershom:b20.1: And why: do they combine to obligate him an offering for misuse? Yom Kippur was in between, and Yom Kippur atoned for him in place of a provisional guilt offering, and it should be like knowledge of uncertainty; let us say that knowledge of uncertainty divides, the prohibition does not combine, and he is not liable to an offering for misuse.
gershom:b21.1: They say: it combines for this reason, that Yom Kippur does not atone for it; for when it atones, it is for a prohibition, but for monetary matters it does not atone. And “he ate today and ate tomorrow” is a monetary matter, since he is obligated in the principal, the fifth and a guilt offering, and for monetary matters it does not atone.
gershom:b22.1: Alternatively, say: Yom Kippur atones for a full measure, for example if he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat before Yom Kippur; but here he ate less than half a peruta, or less than half an olive-bulk, before Yom Kippur; therefore it does not atone.
gershom:b23.1: And so said Reish Lakish: like Rabbi Zeira; and Rabbi Yoḥanan like Rava.
gershom:b24.1: Granted according to Rabbi Yoḥanan: who explains it as a case where he had certain knowledge between each one.
gershom:b25.1: That is why he ties: Rabbi, in the baraita, ties the guilt offering to sin offerings: just as he brings a sin offering for each one when there is certain knowledge in between, so he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one when there is knowledge of uncertainty in between.
gershom:b26.1: But according to Reish Lakish, who says that Rabbi taught that knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings, as we said, where there was knowledge of uncertainty in between and certain knowledge at the end, he should have tied the sin offering to the guilt offering. For with knowledge of uncertainty it is obvious to us that he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one, so he should have said: just as he brings a provisional guilt offering for each knowledge of uncertainty, so he brings a sin offering for each knowledge of uncertainty, since there was certain knowledge at the end, as he holds that knowledge of uncertainty divides into sin offerings. It is difficult.
gershom:b27.1: He walked on the first and did not enter the Temple, and walked on the second and afterward entered the Temple: he is liable to an offering for the impurity, since either way he is impure, for he walked on both.
gershom:b28.1: And likewise, he walked on the first and entered the Temple, and walked on the second and entered: he is also liable, either way. And for [impurity of] the Temple and its sacred items we require knowledge at the beginning and at the end and a lapse of awareness in between, as it is written of them: “and it is hidden from him… and he knows.”
gershom:b29.1: He walked on the first and entered the Temple, and afterward was sprinkled on the third day and again on the seventh, and immersed, and afterward walked on the second and entered: he is liable, for he entered twice, and either way he was impure, either the first time or the second time.
